criteria.name: Q1 Quality attributes
criteria.reasoning: Performance and availability are well justified from the scenario and performance scenario is fully six-part and measurable, but the availability response measure ('stay up most of the time') is not measurable.

evidence.quote: Response measure: the system should stay up most of the time.

criteria.name: Q2 Architectural style
criteria.reasoning: Clear recommendation (modular monolith) with two scenario-specific trade-offs (team size, root causes of known problems) and the downside of the recommendation explicitly acknowledged.

evidence.quote: With five developers, running eight or ten services would mean more time spent on infrastructure than on features.
modules cannot be scaled independently, and a bug in one module can still crash the whole process.

criteria.name: Q3 Availability calculation
criteria.reasoning: Parts (a) and (b) are correct with working (99.30%, 5.0 h). Part (c) is wrong: the student reports only the payment-pair availability (99.9975%) and omits the other three components; correct end-to-end is ~99.80% with ~1.5 h downtime. One part incorrect, method otherwise correct.

evidence.quote: So the new availability of placing an order is 99.9975%

criteria.name: Q4 Resilience pattern
criteria.reasoning: Circuit breaker correctly named and explained (states, thresholds) and applied to the outage, but no explicit drawback or tuning consideration is given beyond an example threshold.

evidence.quote: Students would have seen "payment temporarily unavailable, please try again or pay at the counter"

criteria.name: Q5 Consistency and availability
criteria.reasoning: Both choices justified with concrete techniques (Redis TTL cache; idempotency keys), but CAP is applied incorrectly: partition tolerance cannot be given up; during a partition one must trade C against A.

evidence.quote: for payments we choose consistency and availability and give up partition tolerance

criteria.name: Q6 Architecture decision record
criteria.reasoning: Context, Decision and Consequences are present and scenario-specific, but consequences are one-sided; no negative consequence (e.g. eventual notification, extra infrastructure, duplicate handling) is stated.

evidence.quote: Consequences: Placing an order no longer waits for the outlet, so the response time improves.

criteria.name: Communication and format
criteria.reasoning: Headings, order and IEEE citations/references are correct, but at least two answers (Q2 ~200 words, Q4 ~160 words) exceed the 150-word limit, and no assumptions are stated.

evidence.quote: First, team size versus operational overhead.
The Circuit Breaker pattern [2] would have contained the failure.

technical_issues.issue: End-to-end availability after adding the second payment provider is computed as the payment-pair availability alone (99.9975%); the other three components (0.9995×0.999×0.9995) were dropped. Correct: 0.9980010×0.999975 ≈ 99.80%, downtime ≈ 1.5 h/month.
CAP theorem misapplied: 'give up partition tolerance' is not a valid choice; partitions must be tolerated, forcing a C-vs-A choice during a partition.
Availability response measure 'stay up most of the time' is not measurable.
No negative consequence given in the ADR.

overall: Strong, well-argued answers for Q1, Q2 and Q4. Q3(c) drops the non-payment components, Q5 misapplies CAP, Q6 lacks a negative consequence, and Q2/Q4 exceed the word limit with no assumptions stated. Overall a good submission with fixable technical slips.

feedback.summary: A strong submission overall. Q2 was excellent with scenario-specific trade-offs, and Q1, Q3, Q4, Q5 and Q6 all showed sound method. To lift marks: make the availability response measure measurable, include the non-payment components in Q3(c), apply CAP correctly in Q5, add a negative consequence to the ADR, and keep every answer within 150 words.
next_steps: In Q3(c), multiply the payment-pair availability (0.999975) by the other three components (0.9995×0.999×0.9995) to get the end-to-end availability (~99.80%, ~1.5 h downtime) rather than reporting the payment pair alone.
In Q5, reframe the CAP argument: partition tolerance cannot be given up; during a partition you must choose between consistency and availability, so justify each choice as C or A under partition.
In Q6, add at least one negative consequence (e.g. delayed outlet notification, duplicate-order handling, extra infrastructure) to balance the ADR.
Trim Q2 and Q4 to 150 words each, stating any assumptions explicitly, and make the Q1 availability response measure measurable (e.g. '99.5% uptime measured monthly').

criteria.C1: You chose suitable attributes (performance and availability) with good scenario-based justification, and your performance scenario was fully six-part and measurable. To reach Excellent, both response measures must be measurable: 'stay up most of the time' is not. Replace it with a quantified target, e.g. '99.5% availability measured monthly', and keep the six-part structure for both scenarios.
criteria.C2: Excellent work. Your modular monolith recommendation was clearly justified with two trade-offs tied to the scenario — the five-developer team size and the root causes of the known problems — and you acknowledged the downside (no independent scaling, one bug can crash the process). This meets the Excellent standard; just watch the 150-word limit (see C7).
criteria.C3: Parts (a) and (b) were correct with working shown (99.30%, 5.0 h). Part (c) reported only the payment-pair availability (99.9975%) and dropped the other three components. The end-to-end availability is 0.9980010×0.999975 ≈ 99.80%, about 1.5 h downtime per month. Your method is sound — show the full product in part (c) to reach Excellent.
criteria.C4: You named the circuit breaker correctly, explained its states and thresholds well, and applied it convincingly to the outage with a realistic user-facing message. The missing element for full marks is an explicit drawback or tuning consideration — e.g. false trips on slow (rather than failed) calls, or how to choose the failure threshold and timeout values.
criteria.C5: Both choices were reasonable and you named concrete techniques (Redis TTL cache; idempotency keys), which is good. However, CAP was misapplied: 'giving up partition tolerance' is not an option — partitions will happen, so the real choice during a partition is between consistency and availability. Restate each choice as C-over-A or A-over-C under partition to reach Excellent.
criteria.C6: Your ADR had all three sections, scenario-specific context and a clear decision, and the positive consequence (faster order placement) was well stated. What held it at Proficient was the one-sided consequences: add at least one negative consequence, such as eventual outlet notification, duplicate-order handling, or extra infrastructure cost.
criteria.C7: Your headings, ordering and IEEE citations were correct, but Q2 (~200 words) and Q4 (~160 words) exceeded the 150-word limit and no assumptions were stated. Practise writing tight, prioritised answers: state assumptions in one line, cut generic textbook material, and count words before submitting to reach the Excellent level.
